This family of methods uses sparse data structures (sparse grids, octrees, VDBs) to localize the surface interface and concentrate samples only in relevant regions, effectively skipping empty space to reduce MLP evaluations [S1].

The claim states that the family of methods uses sparse data structures (specifically mentioning sparse grids, octrees, and VDBs) to localize the surface interface, concentrate samples in relevant regions, skip empty space, and reduce MLP evaluations. Source [S1] explicitly confirms all these points: it lists sparse grids, octrees, and VDBs as examples of sparse data structures used to localize the surface and eliminate empty voxel cells; it states this ensures neural fields are only evaluated in non-empty regions (reducing MLP evaluations); and it mentions that sparse voxel grids allow skipping empty regions during ray tracing.
supported

The claim states that empty voxels are progressively pruned during training based on an initial geometry signal. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'They then progressively prune empty voxels during training based on this initial geometry signal.' This matches the claim exactly.
supported

The core challenge in applying sparse structures to NeRF is that surfaces emerge during training, so space-partitioning data structures cannot be precomputed in advance and must be periodically updated [S1, S2].

The claim states that surfaces emerge during training, preventing precomputation of space-partitioning data structures and requiring periodic updates. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'Surfaces typically emerge during training, so space-partitioning data structures cannot be precomputed in advance and must be periodically updated.' Source [S2] corroborates this by stating: 'in the NeRF setting, surfaces only emerge during training... this leads to a more complex training process in which the sparse data structure must be periodically updated.' Both sources fully support every fact in the claim.
supported

supported

Early approaches like NSVF [LGZL∗ 20] and Efficient-NeRF [HLC∗ 22] introduced multistage coarse-to-fine strategies using sparse grids or two-level octrees (NerfTree) to dynamically adapt voxelization to the underlying scene structure [S1, S2].

The claim is fully supported by the evidence. Source [S1] explicitly states that TNSVF [LGZL* 20] (referred to as NSVF in the claim, likely a typo or shorthand for the method family) and Efficient-NeRF [HLC* 22] use multistage, coarse-to-fine strategies. It details that TNSVF uses sparse grids and Efficient-NeRF uses a two-level octree (NerfTree) to dynamically adapt voxelization to the scene structure. Source [S2] corroborates that NSVF [Liu et al. 2020, which corresponds to LGZL* 20] adopts a multistage, coarse-to-fine strategy.
supported

3.  **Refinement:** Use hierarchical structures (like octrees) or sparse grids to cull unused features from dense grids, improving efficiency when the surface of interest is known or can be progressively refined [S2].

The claim states that hierarchical structures (like octrees) or sparse grids are used to cull unused features from dense grids to improve efficiency when the surface is known or can be progressively refined. Source [S2] explicitly confirms this in the passage: 'If the surface of interest is known a priori, a data structure such as an octree... or sparse grid... can be used to cull away the unused features in the dense grid.' It further supports the 'progressively refined' aspect by noting that in NeRF settings, 'regions of the feature grid are progressively refined and culled away as necessary' using multistage strategies. Therefore, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
supported
